utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsels Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us are our legal assistant Miss Adisa Mehic, and our case manager Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I learned with a view to the coming witness, the next witness projected, as such Milosava Nikolic, that this is a lady of 71 years old, and meaning also with a view to her experiences during the war actions and the subsequent actions in which she might testify, that has a great influence on her person. This information confirmed to me is that, well, she need indeed some time as being an elder lady during proofing as well. So if it has been confirmed to you that, upon finalising this redirect, we can start, it should be more defined in we should start upon the demand of the Trial Chamber. And we will do so then. But I advise you strongly to accept that we will start her proofing -- start her testifying tomorrow, as we have then two days. I have been informed that the subsequent witness cannot start earlier, as being contacted by the Victim Witness Unit that his flight cannot be earlier than already arranged for. In sum, Your Honours, I advise you to accept to finalise the redirect and your questioning of the witness today, if so, and then start tomorrow with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your position on this, Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I will be taking that witness. That's why I will respond. As far as the timing is concerned, that's really a matter for the Prosecution and the Court. We don't have a position. We just note that we received at 8.40 this morning an exhibit list. We haven't received proofing notes yet. Our understanding was this next witness was illiterate, so that is already one surprise that there is a list of exhibits for her to be shown. But I will -- I would note the late hour of this being served on us and the fact we don't have proofing notes as not being entirely satisfactory. I also just want to mention that as far as the issues arising in the re-examination of this witness is concerned, the current witness, that I may be taking some of those issues given that there were issues of law which were going to look into, so just to say not to be surprised if you hear from me with the witness who has so far been dealt with by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will decide at the end of the -- when we finish with this witness, what to do. In the meantime, is this witness available? Will she be available here? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours please, the situation is the witness is arthritic and is unable to sit for an extended period of time, which resulted in Ms. Richardson being unable to complete proofing yesterday. And on that basis Ms. Richardson would like to express the preference to commence her evidence tomorrow, the reason being that no loss of time will be occasioned to the Trial Chamber, because the next witness is not available until Thursday in any event, and that's the basis on which we are seeking an extra period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the matter that was raised last time as to the procedural law that should apply during re-examination, the reference was made to the transcript going back to -- during the re-examination of Witness Bogilovic. The position is as follows: I come from a system where we draw a clear distinction between leading questions and direct questions. A leading question, from the system that I come from, is a question that is in a form -- it's put in a form calculated to suggest the answer to it. The position is as follows: If, during the Bogilovic re-examination I used the word "leading questions are permitted," I meant to say not leading questions, but direct questions. I am also making it clear, therefore, that as far as direct questions which are not leading questions are concerned, they are permissible under re-examination. And amongst the direct questions, I am including questions which contain a statement of some facts material to the issue and that the witness -- and the witness is asked to provide a simple, affirmative or a negative answer thereto. That will be permissible. In addition, just to make it clear what I also understand by direct questions which are permissible during re-examination, a question during re-examination is not forbidden on the grounds that it may lead -- or that it leads the mind of a witness to a particular subject if it will tend to elicit in a fair manner the circumstances -- in the circumstances the honest belief of the witness. With regard to the use of a prior statement consistent or inconsistent, there I have to be very categoric. I mean, that's why I did point out during the last sitting that short of you trying to ask the Trial Chamber to grant you the status of hostile witness, you will only be allowed to make use of prior statements to refresh the witness's memory and not to contradict him. The moment you will try to contradict the witness or to discredit him, then I will stop you. All right? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much for that guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I just address you briefly on that subject. It would assist us to hand up copies of small bundles which I prepared because I will also refer to them later, so it's one for each of the Judges and one for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, please, one thing I don't want from you or from Mr. Di Fazio, from Ms. Sellers, whoever, is coming from the common law tradition. This is -- I know -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will become apparent if it will be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Let's not try, during the proceedings, to stick to British law or Australian law or Canadian law or to US law, because in the States, for example, it varies from state to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same applies to questions that Judges can put, including questions during court-martials.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. May I say at the outset I'm the last person who would insist on my own national jurisdiction because I know this jurisdiction better than my own probably, so believe me I'm not going to insist that Archibold should be followed, or the federal rules of evidence, or anything. But of course, certain guidance can be provided by those practices. I pass this up merely because on the memory refreshing exercise there is some guidance on the third page of this handout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, sorry, the third page, I wish to draw your attention to the reference there to the bottom of the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Third page of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of this hand-out, page 1071, paragraph 876.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're referring to the Archibold.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I will just take the pages in sequence just so it is clear why I pass this up. It refers there to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says 1071 at the bottom, where there is reference to the "... twin phenomena within the daily experience of practitioners in the criminal courts. First, a witness statement often bears little --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please slow down, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. "First, a witness statement often bears little relation to the evidence given by the witness. Secondly, a witness who is permitted to have his statement in front of him frequently latches onto it and sticks to it as if it were a script." I wanted to highlight that phenomena, those phenomena because I think this is something which is also of concern to us, that we were concerned to have the best evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- of a witness and of course, he may, if shown a prior statement, in inverted commas, he may feel he has to latch onto it. I wanted to highlight that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're preaching to the converted on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm obliged, Your Honour. The next page 1072, this is still of Archibold, 2002, I handed that up just because there is a summary of the foundation for the memory refreshing exercise. Where it says, "A proper and sufficient foundation will have been laid if the witness gives evidence to the effect, 1, that he did make a statement to the police --" for us that would obviously be investigators -- "2, that he made the statement on such-and-such a date; and 3, that at the time he made it the matters he dealt with in it were fresh in his mind." There is the issue of contemporaneousness, if I can put it that way, contemporaneity, of the statement. In this case we have statements from 1999 and 2001 and they're certainly not contemporaneous with events. Of course, we can come to all of this but I'm just explaining the hand-out really at this stage. The next page, 1141, I handed up just for the reference to "leading questions should not be asked in re-examination." Given what Your Honour said this morning, there is no need to dwell on that. That was also set out in the extract from Murphy On Evidence. And I included that because Peter Murphy practices in the UK and the US, and of course before this Tribunal as well, so I thought that would be useful as a reference to re-examination and that leading questions are not permitted in re-examination for the same reason as in the case, re-examination in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There let me make it clear, the distinction is the following, Mr. Jones and Mr. Di Fazio: What is the ultimate legal consequence should the Prosecution in this case ask the Trial Chamber to declare the witness as a hostile witness? In that instance, from that moment onwards, Mr. Di Fazio can cross examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that witness, that's the basic legal consequence. And if he would be granted the right to cross-examine that witness, then for all intents and purposes he will be put in the same position that you are when you are cross-examining the witness. After that, the examination-in-chief has come to an end, which then, in turn, brings us to another legal conclusion; that if the Prosecution in this case does not seek to have this witness declared by the Trial Chamber as a hostile witness, then at the same time the Prosecution cannot pretend to be in the same legal position as it would have been or as it would be in the case of cross-examining. So the ultimate result is that while leading questions are permissible during cross-examination, they cannot be permissible in re-examination, et cetera. However, our position is as follows:, and this is a position we have reached trying to study the position as it obtains not only in Great Britain -- or in England but in other common law jurisdictions, where especially those where a clear distinction is made between what is classically defined as a legal question sequitur simpliciter and a direct question, which is not a leading question. Obviously, a leading question is always a direct question, but not all direct questions are leading questions. And the distinction exists also in civil law jurisdictions. We are not coming to the conclusion that certain direct questions are permissible because they are permissible under civil law tradition but more so because they are -- the position is so in many common law jurisdictions. But that will be -- in other words it will be us three who will be gauging the situation and each and every question as it arises. The only serious problem that I can foresee is not knowing how Mr. Di Fazio, if Mr. Di Fazio intends to make use of prior statements, and if he does, how he intends to make use of those prior statements. And I'm saying this, because from my experience, I know that sometimes the moment you try something that -- with all due respect, you will then not be allowed to do -- the damage would have already been done. So this is why I'm telling you, I hope we are speaking the same language. If I smell for a moment that you're -- you're going to use the word "abuse," but abuse in good faith, Mr. Di Fazio, abuse in good faith the system, I will jump on you without the least hesitation. And if you try to go beyond the -- I will stop the re-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: If it's of any assistance, if Your Honours please, I've had the opportunity of the weekend to consider the matter. I've gone through it and I intend to re-examine in the usual fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's even better then. MR. DI FAZIO: And if I -- I made a prediction that I would be a substantial period of time on Friday. I have revised that too. I don't think anything is going to arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this, you know as much as I do that irrespective of how the law varies from one common law jurisdiction to the other, at the end of the day answers given to an irregular leading question, to a leading question which should never have been put and unfortunately it has been put and an answer has been given, that answer does not depend on the validity of the question as far as admissibility is concerned, and that is always admissible. And this is across the board in all common law jurisdictions. And this is why I'm saying, don't try to overstep the basics, because we will stop you. Because at the end of the day, apart from the usual principles that are applied upon review as to the materiality, substantive materiality of the irregularity and whatever, we should do our utmost to avoid these things happening. However, I'm sorry, Mr. Jones, I stopped you halfway. I wanted to say something which arose from what you had...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged to Your Honour and obliged to my learned friend for the indication which means a certain number of the submissions which I was planning to make would be premature. We would, of course, still have submissions if Your Honours were to wish to use the prior statements and I would just reserve the opportunity to address Your Honours on that, on that matter, if there were to be an exercise conducted similar to that which was conducted with Dr. Mukanovic, because the concerns are the same from our point of view if prior statements are put to a witness from the Bench as from the Prosecution. In fact, we see the dangers as being worse if the Bench put statements based on prior statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. It's questions, sorry, based on prior statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can bring the witness in. I will explain to him the reason for the delay. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, sorry to -- just as far as the next witness is concerned, are you amenable to starting her tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, given that Ms. Richardson has not yet proofed the witness, finished the proofing, given that the Defence have not yet been given a report on the proofing -- MR. DI FAZIO: And also, Your Honour, given she will easily be completed before we can even get the next witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me finish. Given what was stated both by yourself and lead counsel, Mr. Wubben, then I think we have no option but to accede to your request. On the other hand, although you tell me -- you're telling me that there will not be any problems in finishing this witness before the next one arrives, I have heard what you said, namely that she cannot sit for lengthy periods of time and I would like to know whether that is going to cause us a problem, because if it's going to cause us a problem, the only problem that it could cause us is that we -- in spite of all your statements -- we will not be able or in a position to start with the next witness on time, according to schedule. This is the only problem that I have. I mean, but we are amenable, yes, to start tomorrow. MR. DI FAZIO: I will make sure that Ms. Richardson considers the matter and gets back to us as soon as possible, if that is the slightest danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think there is nothing else that needs to be said. Let's start. Bring the witness in, please, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a quiet weekend and that you managed to rest from the previous days. A well deserved rest. I am sorry that we are starting not at 9.00 but 9:30, but we had procedural matters to discuss, procedural matters that of course do not concern you, they concern the trial, but they needed to be discussed before we could continue with your testimony. Madam Vidovic is going to finish with your testimony this morning and then there will be a short re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio and then there are a few questions from the Bench. And then you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, although this is a different week, you are still testifying under the same oath or solemn declaration that you entered last week. Just a memento of that. I know that you are an honourable man. So you may sit down and Madam Vidovic may proceed with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you have spoken about the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness an excerpt from the war diary, P84, namely pages 50 and 51, which is page 8 in the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about pages 50 and 51, please. Mr. Meholjic, could you please look at the document in its part where you can see the name Osman and where it says: Let us agree on concrete things. Let's give names to the structures or let's assign names to the structure.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 1, yes, I can see that. I can't find the name Osman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is page -- can you see the ERN number, 5051?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5051, I apologise. Osman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the place where it says: Let's give the names to structures. Avdic - president; president of the executive board - Hamdija; secretary - Ankic Esad. The secretary for economy remains the same, the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence - Suljo Hasanovic. The chief of the civilian protection staff - Jusuf Halilovic. The chief of the public security station - Becir (Mirza; VP civilian police - Nurija). Under that, under number 8, it says commander of staff - "Naser (he is not a member of the War Presidency)." In connection with this I would like to ask you as follows: We are talking about a session which took place on the 14th of October, 1992. In addition to Oric's name, it also says next to his name that he is not a member of the War Presidency. Do you allow the possibility that you did not have the information that Oric, as of the 14th of October, 1992, was not a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I will answer, but I don't want to drag anybody into the things that I don't know. I was not present at this meeting and I cannot confirm that he was or that he wasn't. Can you understand me? Can you appreciate that? I believe and I will explain why I believe that, if the Presiding Judge will allow me to say that, that some things were happening in the circumstances that were in place. On the other hand, the things that were happening were beyond our regulations that were in effect at the time. The commander should have been, was supposed to be a member of the War Presidency. I'm not saying anything with that. Mr. Oric and you, if you have documents or if the Prosecution has documents, then you will know that the first War Presidency that was appointed by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is the Presidency in which Oric and I were together in the period after the demilitarisation. I know that and you can find it in one of the official gazettes of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as for this, I have already claimed that this is illegal, this was against the law. Now, whether somebody is offended or hurt by that, it's not up to me to say that. It's up to the Judges to be the judges of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, when you testified that he was a member of the War Presidency during this period of time, you believed that this was supposed to be the case, according to the law. However, you were not aware of the facts. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are, because I repeat again some things which were happening were happening far from me, because I was not allowed access to those things and I cannot say -- I know that he was supposed to be there. He should have been. If he wasn't and if this is a valid document, that's another story, and I cannot dispute that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to show you a different document. I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If I may, another explanation. The Presidency, the War Presidency, that is, had to fill up the structures that were established later, the chief of civilian protection, the president of the court, and so on and so forth, the chief of police, the commander of the Territorial Defence or the armed forces. This is what had to be there. These people did not have to be elected. They were there by virtue of their functions. The Presidency that was in place and that was headed by Mr. Avdic, and when you said that Avdic and Hamdija were the high officials of the SDA, I can tell you that this Presidency made a decision or issued a decision that is unprecedented, and the decision was to ban the work of the Assembly and the political parties. When I joined the War Presidency, I made an effort for this decision to be made null and void and we allowed the Assembly to continue working, and then, then amongst the MPs, Osman Sulic [phoen] was appointed a president of the War Presidency. This was done by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question, and Mr. Meholjic, try to keep your answers as concise as possible, please. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I'm going to show you another document issued by the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality. The date is 13, May, 1994. I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness that document. This is information and requests for the verification of the Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica. The date is 13 of May, 1994. Mr. Meholjic, could you please take a look at this document, and particularly can you please look at page 3 of this document, which is page 2 in the English version. Somewhere around the middle of that document, it says as follows. Mr. Meholjic, you can see that the document is a request for the verification of the Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. On page 3, in the bottom part, it says: "The Presidency of Srebrenica municipality at its session held on the 13, 14th -- 13th of April, 1994 issued a decision on the establishment of the Presidency of municipalities of Srebrenica. In keeping with the decree of Defence, according to that decision, the Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica will consist of the president of the Srebrenica municipality, President Fahrudin Salihovic; chairman of the municipal executive committee, Hamdija Fezic; head of the department of the Ministry of Defence, Suljic Hasanovic; chief of the public security station in Srebrenica, Hakija Meholjic; commander the civilian protection staff in the municipality, this post was not filled. These duties are discharged by the chairman the executive committee. The post of chief of the civilian protection staff has been filled. On the 6th, presidents of Assemblymen's clubs, in the Municipal Assembly, press of the SDA club is Hajrudin Avdic, and he is also a member of the Presidency. Presidents of Assemblymen's clubs of other parties left Srebrenica and currently these clubs do not have representatives in the Presidency. Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. Murat Efendic is also a member of the Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica. At our proposal he was elected by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And finally we have the statement: "We ask you to verify our Presidency as soon as possible." Mr. Meholjic, do you agree with me that the name of Naser Oric cannot be found in this document?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, anybody can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also agree with me that it is a fact that in the municipality of Srebrenica, during that period of time, a demilitarisation was in place and it is that fact that had an impact on the composition of the War Presidency. Is that the reason why Oric's name is not here, that he was not a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question. First of all, I have never seen this document before. Secondly, I am not clear. I don't understand that we did not have the chief of the civilian protection, and I know that the man was there all the time, Jusuf Halilovic. I don't know who drafted this document. It seems that it was Salihovic. I don't see a signature. I don't see anything that would make this document clear to me. This document was issued 12 years ago and it is very hard for me to remember anything about that. I'm not the author of this document and I can tell that he wasn't. Yes, looking at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I want to make sure that I've got the same document. It's been twice now put to the witness that the name Naser Oric doesn't appear. It is on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. You had the explanation, not actually being made by Madam Vidovic herself. I was going to interject -- intervene myself, because, as you say, on the first page there is the inclusion of Mr. Oric in the War Presidency. But on the second page, which is what the question referred to, you have a new phase in the historical events and that is when demilitarisation had just come into force. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And she is actually trying to make the point that I would have tried to make had she not made it, that this seems to be the only explanation why the composition of the governing body in Srebrenica changed on the 13th of April of -- was different on the 13th of April, 1993. However, the point that certainly has been made now and for which there doesn't seem to be an explanation is that this document, under item 5, bottom of page 2, English text, purports to say that the commander of the civil protection staff and the municipality was not appointed, this post was not yet filled. And the witness is saying that his knowledge with demilitarisation, the appointment of Jusuf Halilovic as chief of the civilian protection had not been effected. And that makes him query the correctness of this document. Have I interpreted your testimony correctly, Mr. Meholjic, or not? Have I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic is saying that Jusuf Halilovic was there before and upon -- or after demilitarisation. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to tender this document into evidence, and if it may be given an exhibit number, we will be looking at this document later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- 251. So this document which has been tendered by the Defence and which is dated the 13th of May, 1994, issued by the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality, and with reference number 01-183/94 is being received, admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit D251.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with another excerpt from P84, and this time I would like the witness to be shown pages 50 and 51. I apologise. We're talking about the same pages that we have already shown to the witness. We are going to look at a different part of the excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the part around the middle of the page, where Naser's words are quoted. Can you see it? It is above the part that we discussed a while ago. I'm going to quote. It says here: Naser: All the current problems are due to organisation. Mr. Meholjic, let me just inform you as well as the Trial Chamber that this is an excerpt from the session that was taken -- that took place on the 14th of October, 1992, and Naser said at this session as follows: All our problems are due to organisation. All of this boils down to the fact that everybody should assume their part of responsibility. And later on, you can quarrel about power. Let's all come to our senses. Let us put an organisation in place in order to protect ourselves. It is possible that there is some ammunition in Fakovici and it hasn't been taken. If we want to be a military, we have to have some order and we have to have a command. In connection with this, I would like to ask you as follows: Mr. Meholjic, as far as you know, Oric tried to bring some order into the ranks. He wanted people to come to their senses. Is this what you can read in this part of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I can see. This is what everybody can see. There is nothing in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, do you agree with me if I say that Oric was aware of the fact that people around him, the local commanders and members of the War Presidency, are actually fighting over power? Did he ever discuss that issue with you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here, Naser and I spoke quite a number of times, and we mostly agreed on things. Secondly, he -- even when he agreed not to disagree, he didn't object to hearing my remarks and hearing my views. And I'm sure he will confirm that. In my testimony I've already said that he was surrounded by people who were bad people. But he -- I didn't have the power or the will to deal with that problem, and that is why my main position, which is not of any importance for this Trial Chamber, and that was my reason for him not being in any position, because the situation was complex, there were no institutions, the situation would have been different if the institutions were in place, if there was somebody else who would have called people to mobilisation. Maybe the two of us would have been couriers and nothing else. It was a difficult situation, a complex situation. He was a young man. He was not -- it is not the fact that he was not capable, but he was not experienced and he was not used to dealing with the people the way they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that he was trying to introduce some order in the way that he could? Will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read this and when I remember some things, yes, he did try to introduce order. Whether he could or whether he couldn't is a different issue, but the situation was bad. I wouldn't wish it upon anybody to go through the things that I had to go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with another excerpt from this document, and the page is 5098. This is -- these are the four -- last four digits in the ERN numbers, 5098, and we're talking about the excerpt from the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, the session took place on the 22nd of December, 1992, and this is an excerpt from the minutes of this session. Can you please look at the part of the page where Naser is speaking, and it is the same page that the Prosecutor has already shown to you. Naser brought the meeting to order. He spoke about the mine and I'm going to quote the second part of his speech, which starts with the following words: Our biggest problems is to man the lines and protect our property. The fighters obey their superiors. Mr. Meholjic, will you agree with me if I say that this document also shows that Naser, at that particular meeting, criticised the commanders and he also said that the commanders should be the role models for both their men and the civilians when it comes to protecting property. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "The biggest problem for us is to man the lines and protect property." Does this reflect his position and his attitude towards the protection of property at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect that and there is nothing in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am also going to ask you -- put to you one or two more questions, very short ones. In your testimony, you have mentioned a black Mercedes owned by Ibrahim. Was that Mr. Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have just jogged my memory. Golubovic was the last name. I believe that this was the Mercedes, and Ibrahim wasn't there. He was not there during the war. He was Naser's neighbour from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you have also said that this vehicle, at the beginning of the war, was used by Naser. Are we talking about the beginning of the war, the first months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that I was clear in my testimony. I said that I'm aware of that Mercedes - I don't know what the question was about - Naser used it, I don't know whether it was a petrol car or a diesel car. If it was a diesel, then he could have used it a bit longer because there was no petrol and there was some diesel to be had. I don't know for how long he used it. Later on he couldn't use it. Either he couldn't use it because there was no fuel or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't use it at the beginning of 1993, did he?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say. He used it for a short period of time, between day when he came in front of the Domavija. And actually he drove in it to the meeting with me, and he used it after that only for a short period of time because there was no fuel. There was no chance in hell for him to be using that. We criticised it because he drove a motorcycle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw that vehicle, that vehicle did not have German registration plates, did it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Di Fazio, re-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, if Your Honours please. Just on the timing of the re-examination, as I said I will be shorter than predicted. No problem finishing this morning easily. In fact, if I finish before 10.30, could I have a moment to read through D251, which I saw this morning, in a bit more detail and finish it after 11, if that is suitable to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's only three pages, actually. We can give you five minutes now, if you want. MR. DI FAZIO: No. No. Could we just see how we go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I just want to have a look at it a little more carefully than I have been able to. I just found my transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, on Thursday the 7th of April, you were asked questions by Madam Vidovic. And she asked you this about the decision at Bajramovici, she asked you if the body that was formed there on the 20th of May was a decision that was made by an informal group of people. And you said, "According to my assessment, yes." And then you were asked, "According to the legal provisions that applied then, of the former Yugoslavia, that such a decision would have to have been made by a social political body. Isn't that true?" And you answered, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Let's see how -- because you haven't come to the question as yet. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So far, from my recollection, whatever he has stated is correct. If you are referring to the transcript, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecutor is wrong interpreting my question. I did not ask the witness about the regulations in force at that time. I enquired about the regulations that had been in force until that time. And likewise, I didn't say -- I said -- in fact I said "social political community" which means in fact a governmental body and not -- so the interpretation of the Prosecution is wrong. That was what I was saying about the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having heard Madam Vidovic, could you proceed, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm quoting from transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. And ultimately it is what the witness said which is important -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- his opinion about the legality of the whole structure. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were then asked if you agreed that you did not consider that decision to be binding. And you said you were of the opinion that it had to be done in a different way. You still didn't know if it was legal or not, but your assessment at the time was that it was not legal. And you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were then asked: "In other words, you did not consider that agreement at Bajramovici as a State act and therefore you did not act in line with it." Answer: "No." Are you aware of any decision, any move, any effort, any manoeuvre, on the part of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the republican War Presidency, or any of the authorities at all, to disband the Srebrenica War Presidency, alter its composition? Or bring in other people from outside the Srebrenica enclave and add them to the Srebrenica War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's break it into different parts. Because the first part could be mashed together and answered collectively, but then you jump into a second aspect which is completely and almost unrelated. Anyway, I leave it up to you. You're putting the question, but please split it into at least two or three parts. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I should point out that I have mistakenly referred the War Presidency. In fact, I should have been referring to the Territorial Defence. You were in fact talking about the Territorial Defence when you gave this evidence and I have misled you by suggesting it was the War Presidency. So you were being asked questions about the Territorial Defence. Let me be absolutely clear about that. Now, my question is: Are you aware of any move on the part of government authorities to disband the Srebrenica Territorial Defence or alter its composition in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such moves, because I was not close to them. They may have received such instructions, but I don't know. At a later time, I do have some knowledge of suggestions being made that some people from outside Srebrenica be deployed there, some military personnel be sent to Srebrenica. I think I remember that well. But why that never happened, I don't know, because I wasn't involved. So I would like to ask you not to involve me into things to which I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I beg your pardon. If there were some such moves, there must be documents about that, either in the Tuzla region or in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the command of the army. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about Mr. Oric himself. You were asked: "Do you agree that Naser was elected or selected as the commander because he was young, charismatic and a popular person?" You answered: "I would tend to say people who were discussing the whole issue, they were counting on the fact that he was a member of the special forces with Milosevic and he had some training, because they were given special training, and that's why they felt he could do something. And I think that was the reason, even though I was of the view that the commander did not necessarily have to be a good fighter, but I felt that he had to be able to draw on some life experience and have a different view of life because he was young, lively, and, well, that was my opinion." What special forces training are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Naser was young and the people in the area of Srebrenica didn't know him, because he only graduated from primary school in Potocari and he went to secondary school to Bratunac. Anyway, it must have been somewhere else than Srebrenica. And Potocari, the place where he was born and where he lived is on the very border with the Bratunac area. So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, stop. Go straight to the answer. The question was: What special forces training are you referring to? What special training -- come to that. I'm not interested where he received his primary and secondary education, whether he was known in Srebrenica. Let's go straight to the point and to the question that was asked, because otherwise you are going to stay here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I will finish this. I just wanted to explain to make it clear. As a young man he left for Belgrade and there where he became a police officer. He never worked in the Srebrenica area. And according to our knowledge, or to what people in Srebrenica knew at that time, was that he was a man who was from the special forces had arrived. Whether he in fact was a special forces guy or not in the police in Belgrade, I never knew. And he must have gone through some training for communication and so on, but I also went through some training. But whether all of that is correct or not, I don't know. I said that was probably what made the decision makers to decide in favour of him, but I am -- I may make mistakes also. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. These are your words. I'm using your words, Mr. Meholjic, and I would just like you to amplify and explain your words to the Trial Chamber. "People who were discussing the whole issue, they were counting on the fact -- they were counting on the fact -- that he was a member of the special forces with Milosevic and he had some training." Now, in what way were they counting on the fact that he was a member of the special forces with Mr. Milosevic and had some training? In what way were they counting on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness has just said he doesn't even know whether that is a fact, or not, so how he can speculate about why other people might have relied on something which may or may not have been a fact -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in his testimony he said exactly the same words that Mr. Di Fazio is reading out to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. But he has just explained that he didn't in fact know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can answer the question. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm permitted to do it twice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is the case of putting the question again, Mr. Di Fazio, because I see that the witness is looking at me rather than at you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. That's fine. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your answer was, you would tend to say people were discussing the whole issue. They were counting on the fact that he was a member of the special forces with Milosevic and he had some training, because they were given special training and that's why they felt he could do something. So, please explain to the Trial Chamber how they were counting on the fact that he was a member of the special forces with Mr. Milosevic, that he had some training, special training.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people talked about that in Srebrenica. Naser had come five or six months earlier to work with us and that's what people were talking about. And he also -- he was -- he said that to me, that he had been in Kosovo. But I was also in Kosovo in 1991. And Naser had been a police officer since 1988. Those were the most difficult times. He may know more than I. I know what I heard, and also talking to Zulfo about what made them to choose Naser, the answer was, yeah, well, he was with Milosevic, he knows about warfare and stuff. That's it. I don't know whether this is okay. I wasn't there. I can't corroborate that. I can't give a certificate of him going through certain training or specialisation. Probably some documents can be found, or perhaps Oric himself may be able to tell. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were asked questions - I've just been asking you questions about what happened on Thursday. Then on the Friday you were asked questions about a document, Exhibit P80. MR. DI FAZIO: In fact, could the witness be shown P80. Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please. Yes. Thank you. And your attention was directed to paragraph -- sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment. I've lost my point in the document that I wanted to take the witness to. I can't find it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But in any event this document was shown to you and you were asked questions about whether or not the document reflected reality. And you were asked if Safet Mujic had been your commander. And you were asked if Mr. Safet had ever actually been your commander, and you answered, "Well, there were some attempts to that effect, but I don't know. I would say not. There were attempts at organising that, but I can't really claim that he was my commander because he was never in a position to order me anything whatsoever." Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what attempts were made to organise that, namely, his position as commander over you, and who originated those attempts to organise him as commander.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read through this document a little better. I can say the following: There were some attempts by the staff, but now I realise that this is -- this document is dated 19 September 1995 [as interpreted] and when I was giving my statement, I thought that the current state referred to here was 19, September, 1993. I think that this is something to which they can answer better. You keep asking me questions that I cannot answer. I was opposed to this, and Mr. Oric may be willing to corroborate that, but anyway I'm telling the truth. There was the plan to establish the 28th Division and we wanted to show that we had some forces there, because there were also false reports from Srebrenica. Somebody wanted to boast a little. And those reports did not reflect the real state. Now, I stand behind this with all my moral authority because if I had had all of those forces, we would have been in an excellent position. And I think that Safet was not able to able to assert himself over me as my commander. So it would be as trying to install someone as a judge here who has never finished primary school, because the guy you're talking about didn't have any soldiers. I hope I was clear enough. So this document, I suppose, is correct, but it did not -- does not reflect the real situation in Srebrenica. I don't know what Naser agreed about with the one who drafted this protocol. I was against the establishment of the 28th Division. You know what it means to command a division? It is worse than having a factory with 50.000 employees. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a census.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Meholjic. But I'm merely trying to clarify your answer, your words. You were asked very clearly about the document by Madam Vidovic and you were taken to a part of the document that indicated that the 5th Company, based in Srebrenica, the commander was Hakija Meholjic. And Madam Vidovic put to you: "In other words, according to this document, it would appear that your company was part of the Independent Srebrenica Battalion under the command of Safet Mujic." Now, Mr. Safet has never actually been your commander, isn't that so? Never actually been your commander.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. He's never been commander and I stated already that it was a misunderstanding on my part. I thought this was referring to another period but upon rereading this and finding all the data about the establishment and the structure of the municipality of Srebrenica, it was obvious -- it is obvious from another period. So this report does not reflect the real situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. I'm not actually concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because fortunately or unfortunately this matter arose, came to my mind while the question was being put during the cross-examination. It has never been put to the witness that although -- first of all let me correct this. Because further up on the transcript - I've lost track of it now - it is reported that the witness said, I noticed, that this document is dated 19th September, 1995. It's not dated 1995. I don't know if he said 1995 or it's a -- merely a question of wrong interpretation. It is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 19th September, 1993. It was also never put to the witness that this document is divided into four sections and it is divided into four sections because each section refers to a specific point in time reflecting the events occurring during that particular point in time: The first section on which he was not asked questions seems to cover the period April 1992, to sort of September 1992. The second section, which is on page 3 in the English text, starts, it seems, with the events on early September 1992 and the restructuring that took place then. The third section, which is on page 7 -- page 7 in the English. Page 7 in the English text. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- refers to, again, the restructuring that seems to have taken place towards the end, that is in December, of 1992. And the last section, which is on page 9, section 4, part 4, deals with the creation or formation late November 1992 of the so-called subregion. If you draw comparisons between compositions and structures, during the various time frames covered by these four sections, there are differences. And what -- this would spare us having to put the question later on, if you could perhaps direct your question to the witness, which he has answered, but if you could direct it first to the particular period of time in which it is incorporated in this document, and that is the third phase, and then ask him whether there was any -- whether the situation was, at any time, different during the other time frames that are covered by this document. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it seems that the Srebrenica, for example, forces or Territorial Defence or whatever, the structure in early -- or mid-1992 was different from what it was in October or before December of 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems to have changed also afterwards, but... MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. If Your Honours please, I will do -- I've heard what you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we break now. Look at the document. MR. DI FAZIO: I want to have a closer look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And this is something I myself was going to come to precisely because I think the way the question was put to him, from section 3, part 3 of this document, and the answer he gave when he gave -- when he did on the 7th, is pretty much misleading for anyone who ultimately has to draw conclusions from his testimony. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question was whether Safet Mujic had ever, at any period, been the commander of Mr. Meholjic, and that's why I think that this question is clear enough and couldn't have confused the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You referred him to a particular part of the document. And he had not even had the chance to look -- to have a close look at the entire document while he was answering the question. So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, let's continue. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I was asking you questions about Exhibit P80. Just so that you can follow the format of the document, on the first page you will see that it refers to the first formation structure of the TO, and it then goes on to describe its composition from the 17th of April to October of 1992. At page -- if you look at your B/C/S version and you go to the page that has computer number 5844, ends in computer number 5844, you see that it then talks about a second formation structure. And it is talking about events, as I understand it, on and after the 3rd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. After the 14th of October, 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The changes took effect on the 14th October. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. And you see that also -- you will see that also in the B/C/S version at 5848, where it says: On the 14th of October, 1992 the -- following the commander's orders, units were again reorganised as follows, and then there are numbers indicating various formations and the reorganisation. And if you follow that through, you keep going, turning over the pages, eventually you get to number 4, and that is at page 5846, 5846. Page 6 of the English, if Your Honours please. So that is how it is -- the document is set out. And it would appear at the part of the document bearing computer number 5846 that it is talking about events post 14 October 1992. And you can see there what it says. It says that the commander of the Independent Srebrenica Battalion Safet Mujic, and then it talks about the 1st, 2nd, 3rd company, until we get to the 5th company, based in Srebrenica, commander Hakija Meholjic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. At the part of the document bearing computer number 5846. You see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's what you were asked about by Madam Vidovic in cross-examination. Now, the first question that I would like to ask you is, do you know if there was any military grouping or formation based in Stari Grad led by someone called Enes Ustic? If you don't know, say so. Don't speculate, but just tell us if --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't speculate. This is the same unit that was first under Akif Ustic, who was replaced. The Ustic Akif that we mentioned before, he got killed and then he got replaced by Enes Ustic, and it is correct that he was the one leading these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is Enes any relation to Akif?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were first cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Look, I have the same question now with respect to the 2nd, 3rd and 4th company. Just have a look at the information that is contained there. And my question in respect of those entries is this: Are there -- are you aware of there being military groupings or formations in the various places mentioned with those commanders who were mentioned there; 2nd, 3rd, and 4th?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Ramiz Habibovic. Suad Smajlovic, this is the guy whose nickname was Sosun, and if that was him, then that existed. Sabahudin Jusic, I don't know him, I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, to get back to the question that was actually asked of you in court, Madam Vidovic was asking you about this very entry and about the last entry, the 5th Company based in Srebrenica, you, as commander. That is what she was asking you about. And she asked you if Mr. Safet Mujic has ever actually been your commander. In fact she put it to you that he had not. And you answered: "Well, there were some attempts to that effect, but I don't know. I would say not. There were attempts at organising that, but I can't really claim that he was my commander, because he was never in a position to order me anything whatsoever. So if I may just clarify. There had been attempts as I was saying ..." And then you said, "... yes, there had been attempts to that effect, but I don't think they were successful." Now my question is simply this: What attempts were made to organise Safet Mujic as your commander, the commander over you? What were you talking about when you answered Madam Vidovic's question?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one day this guy Safet appeared and told me that he was my commander, and I just chased him out. I asked him what kind of a commander are you? And then he said that the Staff had appointed him. I did not recognise that Staff. This did not apply to me. Whether this took off the ground anywhere else, I don't know. In any case, it did not mean anything to me. He came to me, to my office to inform me of that. There was no written order to that effect. He was a young guy, and when he came to me, I just threw him out of the office. As simple as that. So when I replied to Madam Vidovic's question, I thought that he was referring to the month of September. However, when I looked at the document, I realised that this report was drafted and painted a nice picture to present to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Supreme Command in order to establish the 28th Division, and that was the sole purpose of this pretty picture that was painted in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You referred to the picture that is painted in this document. And that it was done in order to present it to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Supreme Command. Do you say that because you actually have any hard fact or information that that is what the intent was behind this document, or are you saying that because that's what you -- that is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some talks about the establishment of the 28th Division, and since this is not -- this does not reflect the situation on the ground, I spoke to Naser as the chief of the public security station, I asked him what he was doing, whether these people up there would think that we indeed had a division. Do you know what the division means? I advised him as much as I could, as if I had been his brother. I don't know how he took my advice, but I adhere by what I just said and this was the situation that was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. You were asked -- let me rephrase this. During the course of your testimony you mentioned a place called Azlica during the cross-examination on Friday. You mentioned a place calls Azlica. Where is Azlica in relation to Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of anything like that. It doesn't ring a bell. Maybe this is the area where the subregion [Realtime transcript read in error "region"] was supposed to be organised. I was not involved in any of this. I know that some other people tried to organise something and I am not sure that this was successful. There was always attempts at organising some subregions. I have never heard of this in the region of Srebrenica. I don't know all the places. Maybe you can jog my memory. Maybe you can tell me what happened there. As it is, it doesn't ring any bells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologize. I don't like to interrupt, however, the witness was talking and said, "Maybe it is there where people tried to establish a subregion," and the only thing that was recorded is "region" which doesn't mean anything. And as opposed to a subregion, which means a lot in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Subregion. This is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, both of you, please. The question was a very simple one and it is unbelievable how this witness manages to answer on a tangent all the time. The question was: "In relation to Zaluzje, where is Azlica?" This was the question. It's a very simple question. Azlica.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the original interpretation. The interpretation said whether I know whether there is Azlica or something similar, that's why I said this didn't ring any bells. The interpretation was whether I heard of Azlica or something similar, and I said no. I was not avoiding the answer. I know where Azlica is; it's close to Zalazje in the direction of Sase. And as to the other place with a similar name, I don't know of it. Maybe the Prosecutor can repeat that other name and maybe that will clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was a very simple one and you have answered it now in relation to Zaluzje where is Azlica, and we can look at the map that we have here and it's just a couple of kilometres away, to the south-east of Zaluzje. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour can see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Fine. I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, so in cross-examination you were asked this: "Question: I mentioned a certain battle, and the participation on your and Zulfo's part in a certain battle. Quite simply, Zulfo was free to decide whether he wanted to join in or not; is that correct?" And you answered: "If you're asking a question about Azlica, he went and he lost between three or five people at the very beginning and then he left straight away. He didn't do anything at all. So, yes, he could. He was not accountable to anyone."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it, but... MR. DI FAZIO: Page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which date? MR. DI FAZIO: 8th of April, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 8th of April. MR. DI FAZIO: 2005 of the transcript that I have, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, and I thank you, Mr. Jones as well. Because it's -- we have to rely upon both of you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, when you were giving that answer, you were talking, were you not, about the third attack on Zaluzje that you testified about?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how they should reconcile what you said in your examination-in-chief, to the effect that Mr. Oric was in command of that operation, with this answer that you provided in your cross-examination, namely that Mr. Zulfo was not accountable to anyone.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the question was whether he reported to anybody. At that moment, he did not report to anybody. You're talking about a different place, Razlica is outside of the place where this action took place. Yes, it happened on the same day, but those two places were not close and there was no communication between the two of them. Later on, we learned that Zulfo had withdrawn his men and my men were together with Mr. Oric who was up there. And I'm talking about Zalazje. I am not talking about Azlica, A-z-l-i-c-a. Azlica was the place that Zulfo indeed did abandon, and I hope I've made myself clear. At the beginning I said that when I went to the meeting and when Naser came to meet at Domavija asking whether my men would join, he told me Zulfo's men would not be with us because Zulfo's men are assigned to go to Azlica, and that's how I learned about that. If I hadn't heard that I wouldn't be able to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The action that Mr. Tursonovic was engaged in at Azlica, did it occur on the same day as the third attack on Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that it was on the same day, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far apart are these two places, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how far as the crow flies, but I would say it is about anything between one and two kilometres. It shouldn't be more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is -- again this problem results from not being referred to the transcript. I was checking to see whether in examination-in-chief the witness did say that Oric commanded the attack. In fact the evidence is much more complicated and in fact he never said that Mr. Oric was in charge of the attack. He was asked whether he knew who commanded the attack and he didn't -- he didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This formula has always been, well, if Mr. Oric was there, it would be him who --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There may be some speculation. But if my colleague could refer to each time where the evidence is given, then we can check and see whether that is in fact what was said. MR. DI FAZIO: Page 6808 and 6809 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We need LiveNote references really. We have the computers, we don't have the finalised transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. I do. That's what I have in front of me, I don't have it at the moment, and it's pretty clear what was said then. "Who? Who did they have to obey during the attack? You weren't there. "Well, they had to obey Ziga and Ziga had to obey someone. I mean on the basis of my conversation with Naser, I sent him with Naser and it was up to him to decide who was to do what. They were acting in cooperation, but somebody would have had to command, to be in command, because otherwise the action wouldn't have been successful. "Question: Well, with respect, that makes perfect sense. Do you know who it was, who that someone who would have had to command, do you know who the someone actually was? I'm not talking about the localised actions. I'm talking about the entire operation. "Answer: Well, since Naser was up there, Naser obviously. Who else?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: That's pretty clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can ultimately, at the end of the day, make our assessment. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you've heard the quote that I put, that I have just read out, Mr. Meholjic. Now, my question is this: Bearing in mind what you told the court in examination-in-chief, can you explain to the Court what you said in cross-examination, namely that Mr. Tursonovic went to Azlica, which is part of the Zaluzje attack, he didn't do anything and he wasn't accountable to anyone.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Zaluzje. It is not Zaluzje. It is Zalazje - or at least, this is what I received in interpretation. At that moment... At that moment he did not report to anybody. He was not accountable by anybody. He did abandon this action that he was supposed to be in charge of, but he was not taken to task for that. And when I say he was not taken to task, I mean there were no consequences and this is the kind of responsibility I'm referring to. I'm referring -- I don't know whether he was subordinated to anybody, or not. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me intervene here with a very simple question. Taking into consideration the importance of the attack on Zalazje, which was basically the third time that you were trying, why on earth would someone dream of sending Tursonovic and his men to engage in battle somewhere else and not join in with the forces that were needed on the third onslaught on Zalazje? Why would he go two kilometers away and engage the enemy or engage in an action two kilometres away? I think in military terms I do understand, but I want it from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not trying to lecture anybody nor can I do that. At the meeting that was held in Naser's house, I was not there. I don't know what agreement had been reached. Naser told me that only in the evening, after that meeting. And if you remember well, I was not allowed to attend although I had been invited. Zulfo wouldn't allow me to attend, I left, and I really don't know what agreements they had reached and what they had done at the meeting. I only know what Mr. Oric subsequently told me, and he asked me to give him my men. This is something that I can discuss, this is something that I can talk about in a sensible way. The rest is speculation. I did not attend that meeting, and I don't know what the agreement was, what his strategy was. Maybe somebody else was to be engaged but I wouldn't know that. I only know what Mr. Oric told me later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Move on. You were asked questions by Madam Vidovic about Hamdija -- sorry, about Akif Ustic. Page 13 and 14. And you were talking about the episode where Mr. Ustic went off and acted by himself in an attack and was wounded. And you said this: "Question: In the same way you mentioned yesterday that Akif Ustic went into action on his own initiative and, according to your opinion, without Naser's knowledge. "Answer: He did. And I minded. I mean, I said, okay, if Naser didn't know, fine. But Hamdija and myself, we didn't know either. And we were supposed to be his subordinates, and he doesn't tell his company commanders what he was doing and then he ends up wounded or loses between eight or 12 people in such an action. Well, this was a disaster." And then later in, you were asked by Defence counsel: "Isn't it true that your opinion is that Akif did things upon his own initiative without informing Naser, at any rate without asking for any permission from Naser?" And you said: "Yes. And that's what he did when he went to Zalazje, and he took his men there and about 20 people were killed and he himself was killed. He was just doing everything on his own initiative and that's when he messed up as well." So twice you mentioned that a disaster occurred when a commander acted independently, and on another occasion, he "messed up when he acted independently."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question? Is it -- MR. DI FAZIO: I haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm drawing your attention, Mr. Di Fazio, that while you were reading from the transcript, the witness was clearly disagreeing with what you were reading. So we may encounter a problem with the interpretation of what you were reading or what he said. So we will need to clear that first and foremost. MR. DI FAZIO: I've got the transcript here and it may -- it goes through several interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But the essence of what you were saying was that this fellow, Akif Ustic, acting by himself, resulted in what you called a disaster and what you called "messing things up." Now, did you ever speak to any of the Srebrenica Staff or anyone in the military in Srebrenica about commanders acting independently, resulting in disasters and messing up of actions?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make a few corrections. I was not the superior to Akif. That's not what I said, ever. Akif had actions with his men, about 20 of them, and he attacked a huge area without our knowledge, his nearest co-workers. So I stated that things were being hidden from me and that I couldn't talk about what they were doing. But I know that Akif was acting on his own initiative. And he went -- he attacked Zalazje, not Zaluzje, and he lost some men there. He had gone to that village to fetch some stuff, but he was caught -- he was caught in an ambush by Serbian forces and that's where the losses occurred. So the dead bodies were later on exchanged but things were being hidden from me. I had no contact with those things, and the lady should know that many things were in fact being hidden from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, that's fine. I don't actually need the details of the actual attacks itself. It's your comments that I am interested in.
