You're talking about two occasions, two separate occasions where a commander acts independently and a disaster, to use your words, your words, a disaster results, and secondly when there is a mess up again. So what I'm asking you is this: Did you ever convey any concerns to anyone in the military, in Srebrenica, about the disaster and the messes that were being created when commanders acted independently, or at least when Mr. Ustic acted independently?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ustic was my battalion commander. That's what I said. But at the same time, he was the battalion commander and the deputy of Naser Oric. So they should know better. He was my superior, so he was not obliged to inform me. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have something radically wrong with the interpretation here, because it's... I mean, it is obvious that your question was not interpreted well to the witness. I don't believe that the witness did not understand it. MR. DI FAZIO: I will try. I will try a more direct approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. If you're not successful, I will do it myself. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's a very simple matter, Mr. Meholjic. You're talking about Akif Ustic and you've given two examples where he goes off and acts by himself independently, and in both cases you describe the results as either a disaster or messing up. Now, did you ever speak to the Srebrenica TO or military commanders in the Srebrenica enclave about precisely that, commanders acting independently where disasters result and situations are messed up? That's all.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. They all knew what was going on, and so did Mr. Oric. It was not my obligation to inform anybody of such things, because they were not trifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on. MR. DI FAZIO: Page 25, if Your Honours please, of the transcript. Again from Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you able to follow, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, with those references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I would just remind you of the evidence. "Question: There were no circumstances or conditions in place that would enable the commander to exercise the effective control over the troops that were supposed to be subordinated to him? "Answer: No." Question, I think it should be: "When you say 'no,' does that mean that you confirm my statement? "Answer: Yes, I do. There was nothing in place to provide for an efficient control. Not even the organised -- something -- of the United States cannot control all of its troops, let alone us. We were not organised. Secondly, there was no corps. There was no mechanism to punish a soldier. You could only beat him or chase him out of your ranks. There were no institutions as such in place." Now, you've testified about going to meetings of the Srebrenica TO for pre-planning sessions and on other occasions sending Velid, your subordinate, to such planning sessions. As far as you are concerned or you are aware, were those planning sessions designed to organise and marshal forces during the course of attacks?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not really clear, but I will answer it to my understanding. At the meetings I attended, responsibilities were given out for actions -- for future actions. But I was not present when that was done. I was only informed we had a meeting today, we're going there, you're coming from this side, the others will do that, and the third guy will do this, and that was all. There was nothing for me to say or comment about that. So I was not present at meetings where decisions were made about the -- about what should be done against someone and how. So I didn't partake in that. I only was included later -- involved later. I don't know whether I was clear enough. If the question had been clearer to me, I may have been able to give a clearer answer. I've answered to -- to the best of my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The general thrust of your evidence both in-chief and in cross-examination was that the fighters in the Srebrenica area were poorly equipped. My question is this: Were these planning sessions, the ones that you attended -- the few that you attended -- were they attempts, or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. did you observe any attempts to organise and control, through those planning sessions, what was going to happen during the actual attack itself? Military action, whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably about matters of control, what should be done at some place, yes. But about uniforms or other provisions, there was no discussion about that. I don't know if I understood you well. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. We'll move on. Page 30 and 31, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were being asked questions about men coming and going from your units and asking about -- questions about the fighters. And then you were asked this question and gave this answer: "In other words, in Srebrenica, in the course of 1992 until the demilitarisation, people acted on a voluntary basis. Am I right in saying that? And that this was the case even up to the end of the war? "Answer: Yes." Now you appear there to be saying that the fighters under your control and within the enclave, the Srebrenica enclave, right up until the end of the war, acted on a voluntary basis. In the action in Zalazje, were your men free to leave the action at any time that they wished during the course of it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may, I would like to clarify. Voluntary is, if you want to be a soldier, all right. A soldier in the army, for lack of a better word. But if you become a soldier, then there must be order, otherwise it would be chaotic. If you want to be a soldier under my command, all right. If you don't want to, get lost. About volunteers, it's -- the matter is that if someone decides to leave, I have no way of holding him back. I'm not sure about these -- this linguistic point. There is this -- voluntary participation is one thing, and the other -- another thing is being drafted by the State. But even when you join as a volunteer, you must obey certain things, do things that are told to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wonder if you can take it a step further and save me having to put the question later on. Taking you back to the question that Mr. Di Fazio asked you. You've answered that this volunteer system, voluntary system basically boiled down to the ability of an individual to decide whether to form part of your unit, or not. And no one was forced to become part of your unit. And that I have perfectly understood. Now, let's take it to a step between what you were asked by Mr. Di Fazio, that is: Once a soldier under your command is engaged in an action, can he, at that point in time, during the action, decide to withdraw simply because he is a volunteer and not a regularly enrolled soldier? And I take you back to the time when you are going to ask that soldier to form part of the unit which will be engaged in the attack tomorrow, or today. If you asked that soldier: Tomorrow you are going to be engaged in the action that we are going to have in Zalazje, was he free to tell you, Mr. Meholjic, or Capo, Commander, I'm very sorry, tomorrow I can't, I will not join the unit tomorrow? Or had he to obey your command, your order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking only about my men. No, they were not -- in no position to refuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, I just want to... Okay, thank you. Page 32, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were -- very shortly thereafter, you were still being asked questions about this topic by Defence counsel. And you were asked this question: "It is a fact, is it not, that local commanders kept their command of their men? "Answer: I know that I did." Firstly, on that particular point, I will just repeat the question that was put by Madam Vidovic and see if you can provide an answer: "Is it true that local commanders -- not just you, but other local commanders -- kept their command of their men?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's two things, really. One, I think this is would be an appropriate time to caution the witness not to speculate obviously. It's only if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has been told several times and he knows because there were many occasions when he said, "There is no speculation. I won't speculate" without being prompted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Secondly, I remember when this question was put, I'm not sure if the interpretation was perfect, but in any event the emphasis was -- kept on about their men and as for the next question as well, had power over his men. The emphasis was not on had command but had command over their men only, in other words. That was the question which was put, the gist of it. MR. DI FAZIO: Not the question that I see written here. I see it written in black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a difference, definitely. MR. DI FAZIO: There is a big difference. Another question that is here in the transcript: "It is a fact, is it not, that local commanders kept their command of their men?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Obviously the original question was in Bosnian so as to emphasis and just the exact wording, if there is a dispute we might need to go back to that, but as to where the emphasis is placed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can go back to the recording, about there is nowhere else or nothing else that we can go back to. But for the time being, if that is what the transcript says, that's what your question will relate to. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that's not the case, in other words if the witness remembers that that was not the question that was asked of him, then he's free to say so. I mean, it's... He's the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you've heard that. The question was: "Is it a fact that local commanders kept their command of their men? "Answer: I know that I did." Now my question is this, what about the other local commanders, did they keep their command of their men?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they kept it anyway, because when they accept to go into an action, they were in a position to rely upon being able to lead their men into the action, otherwise it wouldn't have made sense. But I wasn't in -- didn't have contact with other people, nor did they contact me, in such a way as for me to know that there was disobedience anywhere. They must know about those things better than I. Where I can say or talk about things, I will. But I won't speculate. There were people deserting. There was all sorts of things going on, but action was taken against them. So I am not trying to duck the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio, I'm sorry. But did the situation fluctuate, vary, at any time between -- the situation that you are describing, was it always the same throughout the period April 1992 to April 1993, or did it change? Did it fluctuate? Because we are talking of a whole year, an entire year here where the structure itself changed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you. As time progressed there was better order. So as time progressed, things got better and we knew more than before, so things were improving, in my opinion. Because at the beginning there were instances where I didn't accept and then later on I did accept some things. So there was -- discipline was going stronger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When would you say, at what particular period of time -- again we're talking of between April 1992 and April 1993 when you have the demilitarisation, during this year, when did the situation that you described really start changing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, really it was in autumn when it started getting better. That's my opinion. And in autumn until the Serbian offensive, then things were getting loose again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, back to you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Next question you were asked was this: "Realistically speaking, Naser had real command, command power over his men, did he? Or did he not? "Answer: Yes, he did. He had power over his men. He did not have power elsewhere." Now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber how they should consider that evidence in the light of your evidence in-chief where you said that in the Zalazje action you subordinated your men to Mr. Oric's command.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you well, there are two questions here. One is whether Naser Oric exerted control over his men, and I meant that men from Potocari and I answered "yes" to that question, and I also added that I had control over my men, who were at the Domavija with me. The other question was, if I understood you well, how or whether I had subordinated my men to Mr. Oric, or maybe the -- or perhaps it would be good for you to repeat that question to me. I'm not sure I understood it well, the second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. You were making a distinction. You were asked about command power over his men, did he have it, and you said, yes, he did. He had power over his men, but he did not have power elsewhere. Now in the context of the answer, correct me if I'm wrong but I assume you were saying, he did not have power over other armed forces or grouping within the Srebrenica enclave. That's the obvious reading, I suggest. So that's what I'm asking you about: Power over other armed groupings in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is still unclear to me, but here is what I said: Direct control, this is what I tried to distinguish, but I wouldn't have participated in the action if I hadn't been clear about what was whose responsibility. If -- so it had to be clear who was authorised to say, let's stop the action. Could I say let's stop? So what -- I don't know what they agreed in the Staff, but what the Staff -- what the Staff assigned to me as my responsibility, then I did it or sent my men to do it. And so Naser could have said, "Let's retreat, guys. No go." There was nothing unclear about that. At that moment, Naser had control over my men to, as for example, order a retreat, and they would have obeyed. I hope I was clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were. You were very clear in examination-in-chief. I don't have any problems. I understood what you said and you seem to have essentially repeated what you said. It's what you said in cross-examination that I'm concerned about. You said this: "He had power over his men. He did not have power elsewhere." Now, in the Zalazje attack that you've spoken of, he had command control over your men, did he not? Now was that the only occasion that you know of where Mr. Oric had command power over other men? Is that how we are to understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There are two questions. I don't know which one he wants the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see whether he can answer them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't understand. Whether on other occasions he had control over other people. Every commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will cut it short. Just one more sentence: Every commander is the person who is most responsible for his men, and those who were subordinated to the TO staff should have been under control. Whether they in fact were or were not, I cannot say. He knows best whether he was in a position to control everybody, or those people on the Staff. I am trying to say -- or I -- that I have been far from the Staff. I haven't participated in the decision. I wasn't allowed anywhere near. Because the crucial question about the establishment of the subregion and so on, nobody ever asked me about that nor involved me in any way. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Page 43, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were being asked questions by Defence counsel over the influence that Naser Oric had as a commander. And you were asked this: "If we set aside for a moment the influence that Naser Oric would have had to have as a commander, keeping in mind his actual influence, could you agree that his influence on the occasion of these meetings, the meetings that you yourself attended, was not greater than Zulfo's, for example?" And then you answered: "If I may, I would just like to point out -- I'm going to answer your question. When I said it wasn't --" I will take you to -- I will take you to the relevant portion of the answer. You answered this: "This is why I said in the beginning that Naser Oric was not the person who was the appropriate choice of commander, because there were problems with people. You had to get them under control. I had no -- there was nothing personal I had against him but I felt it was a bad idea to put a person in that position and he was not up to it." Now the part of the answer that I am interested in is this: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why it was necessary to get them under control? And I take it you're referring to the TO Staff. Explain to the Trial Chamber why it was necessary to get control of them.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand your question. However, if we are talking about Zulfo or anybody else, I believe that there should have been discipline. Discipline should have been put in place. There should have been rules applied, military court should have been established, as well as the structures of civilian authorities, and that would have guaranteed a success, because every discipline is a guarantee of success. However, things were done in quite a disorder and it was pointless for anybody to take things upon themselves without being able to carry things through. And this did not have a bad reflection on the Serbian forces, it had a bad reflection and consequences on us, because we were not organised and it was the Presidency and the TO Staff which largely contributed to our state of lack of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If you will turn to another area you were asked questions about the court system and legal system, if any, that was in place in Srebrenica in the relevant years. Madam Vidovic asked you this: "It is true, is it not, Mr. Meholjic, that you would have filed criminal reports for the crimes, including war crimes, providing that you had any sort of reliable information and evidence to the effect that these crimes had been committed irrespective of the fact who had committed them. Am I right? "Yes, you're right. But somebody would have had to inform -- inform me about that. I would have had to obtain information in order for the investigation to be carried out." So, Mr. Meholjic, if you had been informed that in the Srebrenica enclave Muslim fighters were murdering people, setting fire to barns, slaughtering pigs, setting fire to people's houses, would you have investigated that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have, if the military command had provided me with some information. They were supposed to assist me with that. We took upon ourselves a huge responsibility since there was no military court, there was no military police until later on. And the situation was that we had the army, but at the same time we didn't have the army. It's a very complicated issue and it's very difficult to explain things in light of the circumstances that were in place. But, to answer your question, we certainly would have done something. Maybe we wouldn't have done things completely, but we certainly would have done things, even under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. There are some questions from the Bench. I would invite first Judge Brydensholt. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I'm going first to ask you about the attacks where you or your men participated. Were you told, when you were asked to participate or to provide men for such an attack, were you told what is the goal, what should be achieved during this attack? You have mentioned, as far as I remember, two things. One was to get some food for your own men but also for the general population in Srebrenica. You have also mentioned that a goal could be, on other occasions, to enable people who has been living away from their homes to return to harvest and probably to live there in order to diminish the pressure on Srebrenica. First of all, is that rightly understood? Are those goals which you were told and were aware of?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I knew and these were the goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Were there other goals? For instance, as part of making it possible for Muslims to return to their own homes, to make it impossible for the Serbians to return to their villages? Was that a goal which were discussed?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing: Our mentality and the curse of that people, irrespective of their religion or -- is such that it was very difficult for Muslims to return to a village if that village had once fallen and if there were Serbs in the vicinity. I'm not saying that all the Serbs are criminals, but the Muslims would be afraid that maybe the following night they would be attacked. And the same applied to the Serbs. I claim that none of us have -- nothing against the Serbs. We did not take to the arms in order to cleanse the territory. We took to the arms in order to survive and to save our hides. I was not even interested in whether the state of Bosnia would survive. What I wanted to do was to leave Bosnia, but if we are talking about Voljevica and Zalazje, those are two Muslim places. And people who were in my unit and in other units wanted to go back to their homes. They wanted to be able to continue living there. They wanted to continue their defence in their respective villages, and I believe that I have already said that in my testimony that at one point an issue -- an order had been issued that all the people from these areas should withdraw and form their own units, because they insisted on that and this was allowed to them. They were given weapons. I know how it was in my unit. I complied with the orders of that Presidency. I didn't think much of them, but I gave them my men and they went to the vicinity of Bratunac. They were there for a while, then they were attacked and that's how it all ended. They were expelled and that was it. I don't know whether I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When your men participated in an action, were you aware that civilians -- not soldiers -- civilians were following your men during an attack? Did that happen? Was this regular?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: I don't know what the number of the document is that was provided to me, but when we're talking about Fakovici where I did not participate but I had participated in the meeting, I said at that meeting that the action -- that there had been a leak about the action. The people, because there were so many problems, they followed us with bags in order to look for a piece of bread and that's how we ended with problems with the dead and the wounded, because people are following us with bags in order to get some food. And I believe that this was our best attempt to organise horses and other things, to help these people. But the people just started moving even before us. I did not participate in the action, but I was observing the situation closely and I believe that as many as 5.000 people with bags, like carpet baggers, went to the area in order to get some food. It was very chaotic. It was not organised. Although it was the best attempt at organisation. Maybe if those things had been prevented from the very start, maybe the civilians would not have taken part in those actions, but once the floodgate was open, there was no stopping it. Although, for example, a soldier sleeps at home and says to his brother, his wife: Tomorrow there will be an action so you can join to get food. Everybody knew when the action would take place. There was no secrets. There was a leak every time, before every action. It was a public secret, so to speak. And then sometimes they would leave a day before us, they would spend the night in the woods. They would hide in the woods. They would sit there and wait for the army to launch the action. Sometimes they would be here much more -- much before the army. They knew about the action sometimes even before the rest of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Then I will turn to the situation regarding the prisoners in Srebrenica. You said that you, in this period during the war in 1992/1993, you were not allowed to enter the SUP building, the police building. Is that rightly understood?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Why was that? Could you explain that to me, why could you, as a commander and a former police officer, not go to this particular building?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't go because in that situation I was considered a Serbian man. I don't know what. There are lots of discord, and that's why I said that many things had been hidden from me. When I say "many things," I mean I don't know what had been agreed. I was not clear on things. I was not desirable. And some people even considered me a good target. I was supposed to be murdered on several occasions. My view was that I should move as little as possible and that I should not go there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Were you aware that from a certain time in the autumn of 1992 there was a distinction -- at least from that time, there was a distinction between civil and military police and where, if that was so, were they placed?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while everybody was in the police station and then for a while they were divided. Some of them were close to the corps. But I don't know exactly. In any case, they were under one roof when I arrived. When I arrived to take over the police station, that's when they were all under one roof. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes, they were under one roof. Were they on separate floors? Was there any separation at all between military and civil police, as far as you could see, in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say this, but I did not arrive at the police station. I arrived at a pigsty. There was no inscriptions on the doors; there was nothing there. Nothing. Believe me. When I arrived, I did not come looking for money. There was no money to -- there. I wanted to restore order. There was no order, and I wanted to restore order because I live there. When I arrived there, I did not even have to take my appointment as the chief. I first came to talk to Rashid, who was the head of the crime squad before the war, and Ibro, who was the police commander even before the war. I wanted to hear from them that we would be able to set up a team the way I wanted it. If they had not agreed to that - and they did - I would not have joined the police station. Taib is still alive. He was there before my arrival. He was a member of the police for four or five months before my arrival. He was the commander of the civilian police. He replaced Nurija. That's what I found there. I talked to him. I asked him whether there were any papers, any documents, anything. There was no paper trail of what had been done. As when I was finally appointed, when I took the duty, I reported to the minister of the Drina district, the minister of the interior, whose name was Hazim Vrancic. I used the communication means to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Then there was -- I understand that before the war you didn't have any prison in Srebrenica. You said that. But then a prison was organised behind the court building, as far as I understand. Do you have any knowledge who had the responsibility for that place? You mentioned -- you have used the word "the prison police." Did you have any specific prison police or is that something you just thought of but didn't know? We have not heard of any prison police before.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I've told you in my testimony. When I arrived and when I became the chief of police and when I joined the Presidency, I asked for a court to be established through the minister of justice, and I also wanted the prison police to be established by the minister of justice. The Ministry of Justice issued a decision appointing judges, the Prosecutors, and the police. The commander of that police was a teacher. I can't remember his name, but in any case, he was commander of the branch of the Tuzla prison, because in the former system all the prisons belonged to the respective courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware what you have explained regarding the period after April 1993. But during the period before that, who was, in your opinion, responsible for what was going on in what was used as a prison? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Who was responsible? Well, it should have been the Presidency and the staff. If there had been a prison, I don't know where it was. I don't know where the prison was, if there was any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I just would like to come back once more to the recruiting of groups. You told us that about 60 to 100 men followed your command. And how did you recruit these people? How did you mention that you got these people together?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony, I said that most of these men were reserve policemen. After the ultimatum when we were asked to hand over our weapons, we decided to take to the woods. I did not recruit anybody. Everybody could go home, surrender, flee, or whatever. But one group of people took to the woods with me and this is the core of my future unit. This is not recruitment. A few of them later on fled to Tuzla, some went home, some came to ask me whether they could join me. I said, yes, of course you can. And that's how things happened. There was no recruitment as such. I did not recruit anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: We also heard about other groups. To your knowledge, did they come together or get together in the same way as your group?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they did that, how they recruited people. In any event, I believe that it was all on a voluntary basis because there was no institution that could have mobilised people. How they mobilised people, did they force them to join or not, I don't know. I've told you already that every movement was difficult. It was very difficult to move about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But even if it was on a voluntary basis to join you or to join a group, you testified that it was possible to chase people out of a unit. Is this to be understood in a way that you -- it was on your decision to accept somebody as a member of your group, or not to accept somebody as a member of your group? And if you did accept them, if somebody behaved in a wrong way, that you could say "stay out of my unit"?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now although you told us your people, your fighters did not have uniforms, now you also testified that civilians would follow certain actions. Now, how was it possible to distinguish men who had been members of a unit from other civilians? Was it possible at all? And if so, by what means did you distinguish them?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew my men personally. I've also explained in my testimony that whenever an action was launched, we had agreed on a band that would be worn, a band of a different colour that would be tied around the arm. And that's how the army was marked. I mean, civilians could have done that as well. Nobody prevented them from marking themselves in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, according to the testimony, it was they have not been in barracks, but if there was an action to be performed, how did you get in touch with each other? How did people learn that they should get together in order to have some sort of action?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the others. In my case, there was no problem. I had to issue my men with a written notification. Nobody could leave without a written notification signed by myself. I don't know about the others, how they did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the cross-examination, you have been told or it was understood that there were agreements with regard to getting together to have certain actions. And then you have been asked: There was no line of command? And your answer was: "There was no line of command for me." Now, why did you stress "for me"? Does this mean that it may have been different with regard to other people, other group leaders or commanders?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, war is an evil. Nobody needs a war. One needs to survive in war or sell your hide as dear as possible. When we took our men into action without any prior reconnaissance, then people died. If people placed their lives into my hands, it was my responsibility not to take them into any madness. I didn't like the way things were done, because I believe that the Staff was supposed to prepare every action with everything that it entails. And when the commander is convinced that everything is in place, then the commander should issue an order that an action should be taken and that his men should participate in it. In Srebrenica, in 1995, we had casualties because we did not have good men out there. If we had been organised in a better way, I'm not saying that Srebrenica would not have fallen, I'm saying that a lot of more people would have been saved. When I asked a gentleman from the armed forces what plan was in place for an attack on Srebrenica, they said they did have a plan, that it was secret. In 1995, when I was invited by the Presidency to the PTT building, Ramiz was sitting there, he was sitting and substituting for Naser, and he said that there was no plan at all. And Ramiz was the one who prior to that said that there was a plan but that it was a military secret. I was very cross. I was very angry, but what could I do at that moment? So I'm talking about my part. I believed that my way of thinking of the misfortune that had fallen upon us, it was good. I have given a lot of statements in my life and I'm still here, but my men are not here. My men who have survived are sitting at home and I'm going through all of this once again. I was aware at that moment that I -- that there would be some responsibility discussed at one point. I had that in mind and I -- I made sure that I directed my men well at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the attack or the event of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I have -- I am going to suggest -- it's 12:30. I was going to suggest that we finish with the questions that Judge Eser has to the witness. I do not have any questions to the witness myself. Maybe perhaps one. Probably not, not even that. And after that, we can conclude. But that would involve proceeding for -- how many more questions? About five minutes or ten minutes, maximum more, rather than have a break now and start again in 25 minutes' time. Is that agreeable to everyone?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may correct the transcript. If I understood the witness well, he said "I asked men from the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want a confirmation that we can go ahead for another ten minutes without a break, and I need to get the go-ahead from the interpreters. Okay. I see the interpreters okay. Technicians. Okay. All right. Staff? Right. Let's proceed. Let's hear what Madam Vidovic wishes to point out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a correction in the transcript. I understood that the witness said as follows: "I asked a gentleman from the Presidency whether there was a plan in place in case of a large-scale attack." In the transcript here, it says "in the military command," which is an entirely different story. Can the witness clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked at the meeting of the Presidency whether -- meaning the military command -- whether there was a plan for a special situation such as the attack on Srebrenica or the evacuation of the population. They said, yes, there is a plan but this is a military secret, you can't know it. I had always doubted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Back to my question with regard to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will come back to my question with regard to Fakovici. And I refer you to your testimony where you tried to explain why you did not participate. And you testified: "I mean that it is not a defence operation, but you have to do what you have to do. But if you are attacking, you have to make sure that you have as few victims as possible." Now, what is the difference between a defence operation and an operation which has to be considered as an attack? What do you mean by this distinction?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you attack someone, then it's you who does the planning. So how -- what you do to have as few casualties as possible. But when I'm attacked I must defend myself, and I don't have a plan for that because it wasn't me who decided when that attack would take place. Do you understand now? Is it clear? So when I planned to attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now if you have a defence operation, it is clear, you want to defend something. Now, if you have an attack, what is the purpose of an attacking action? What is the purpose of the attack? Or what was the purpose of the attack?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends from case to case. Talking about Fakovici, the purpose was to provide food, because there were cereals there and our people were hungry. But not at any price, not at any price. So if I can't break through to the place where I was supposed to go, Sefik Mandzic was killed who went there with his men instead of me and they achieved nothing because they got killed immediately and I didn't want to go through a minefield before de-mining it. It was my opinion that the action had not been prepared as it should have been and I decided not to take my people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Who was supposed to take the food? The fighters or the -- some other people? Who was supposed to fetch for the food?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about this concrete case, I think it was the secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence, because under our regulations he was in a position to mobilise men and horses, and whoever had a horse received an order from the secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence, because it was his responsibility to mobilise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to Kravica: You also said it was an event where you did not participate, and why not? Why did you not participate?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, Naser just told me, not at the meeting but while we were sitting down together, that it would be good, since there are many fighters would go, it would be better for me to stay at Srebrenica because there was a possibility of an attack on Srebrenica, so that I could defend Srebrenica. So I wasn't involved in either the preparation or anything else with regard to Kravica and I had no contacts about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, there was also some testimony with regard to the UNPROFOR people in Srebrenica in the first quarter of 1993. Are you aware who was leading the negotiations with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well probably the Presidency, Naser and Ramiz. I have no idea who it was. I was far. I was out there in the field. And my responsibility stopped far out. And I never came to town. Of course, it couldn't have been everybody, so only somebody would, of a certain importance, and it was then the Presidency, staff, and so on. So this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Can I deduce from the questions that you yourself have not been involved in this negotiations with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was ten kilometres away from Srebrenica, on the line which I commanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now another question with regard to the election or selection of Naser Oric as commander. You have been asked by the Defence the following question, page 6932: "Do you agree that Naser was elected or selected as a commander because he was a young, charismatic and popular person?" Then you would answer: "I would rather tend to say people discussed the whole issue..." And your answer seemed to have been rather evasive. So may I put it again. It has been asked whether he was elected because he was a young, charismatic and popular person. Can you - would you confirm this and, if you can confirm it, why he was considered a charismatic and popular person.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. The people didn't really know him. Maybe later on. But at that time we can't really say that he was popular. He may have been popular with some people but not on the whole territory. No, there wasn't anyone who was popular all over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: You were referred to an exhibit which was referred to by the Defence, that is Exhibit P162. It was information given to the president of Tuzla district, signed by Hajrudin Avdic of May 25, 1993. And it reads as follows -- so Exhibit 162: "Faced with that reality, responsible individuals led by our legendary commander, Naser Oric, organised the people for the Defence, at first in the form of sabotage groups and village guards, and later gathering armed forces and creating military and later civilian authority structures on the free territory of Srebrenica municipality." So it was a quotation from an exhibit you had already dealt with. Now, would you confirm, could you confirm what was written in this document?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I can confirm that, this is what it was or this is what it wasn't like. I don't understand the question. If we're talking about the beginning of May, how can you talk about a legendary commander, because he hadn't done anything yet to become a legend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The statement is May of 1993. Not -- 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's -- May 1993 is when the document was issued by...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you like to add anything? If you have realised that this statement was made 1993, you already had one year of fighting within the area of Srebrenica, that you could confirm the description which was made of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I do not hold that opinion. I've always contested it. Whoever wrote it obviously thought otherwise. That's not how I see it. I wouldn't have put it that way, certainly, if it's my opinion you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I have one question for you, Mr. Meholjic, before we send you home. You mentioned in the course of your examination-in-chief and also in the course of your cross-examination that there were, at times, you had, in the Domavija hotel, stocks of foodstuffs. How did you procure that foodstuff?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you. We -- at the Domavija there was some food. Later on, when we went into action, we had a platoon of people who were in charge of collecting food. Others would go looking for weapons, and that's how we proceeded. When I came to Podravanje, I saw many pumpkins and I said come on, take those pumpkins so we can made bread, pumpkin bread, and this is how we procured food. And there was another way. I had several engineers with me, electronic engineers and others, so we set up a workshop that produced a generator to drive a mill to grind food. Because at the time there were no mills. Only later on some people made some. And this is how I procured food. You go to a field. It's full of unpicked corn. We pick it. And this is how we procured food to our fighters. And some people took food home, but not my people. We did it in an orderly fashion, and that's how we went about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware whether the other units that took part in the various actions that were mentioned to you, also had the same structure like yours did? In other words, you had -- would they have a platoon of people who -- that would be in charge of collecting food and another platoon of people that would go looking for weapons? Was this something particular to your unit only or was it common to others as well?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others would collect food all together, load it on a truck and later sell it because food was expensive, but that's not how I did. I never sold anything. I didn't care for making money, I only wanted us to survive. Some commanders actually engaged in smuggling and stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. Okay. Mr. Meholjic, we've come to an end. We promised you we would finish by the end of business on Monday and we have finished even before that. The staff of the Tribunal will now help you to arrange for your return back home and everything will be attended to. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and on my own behalf, but also on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case instituted by the Prosecutor, Madam Prosecutor, against Naser Oric, and also on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher will now escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will continue tomorrow morning, 9.00. I hope Ms. Richardson will have finished with the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might it be also the afternoon instead of the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is in the afternoon tomorrow, I see. Thank you. Yes, tomorrow afternoon. We will start -- I want to make sure that you liaise a little bit with the Victims and Witnesses Unit, if the next witness has got problems because of age or physical condition, please, I want to make sure that her stay in the courtroom will be as comfortable as possible for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've been informed that they already took care in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. I assumed that before I spoke, but I wanted to make sure. So I thank the interpreters, I thank the technicians, the staff and counsel, of course, for having cooperated making it possible for us to finish now at 10 to 1.00 and I will see you all tomorrow afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of April, 2005 at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
